summary.text: At the wedding of Peirithous and Hippodameia, wine maddened the centaur Eurytion and the brawl became a war — Caeneus the invulnerable Lapith buried under pines, Theseus fighting with an axe, and the shaggy centaurs driven at last from Mount Pelium.

chapters.title: The feast and the wine
chapters.text: Peirithous, king of the Lapiths, took Hippodameia to wife and invited the centaurs of Thessaly to the banquet — among them the wise Chiron's wild kindred, born of Ixion's cloud. Homer says it was wine that made foolish even the centaur glorious Eurytion: when his heart was maddened with drink he wrought evil in the house of Peirithous, and grief seized the heroes. Ovid spreads the hall with mixing-bowls and the scent of roasts; the centaurs, unused to feasts of men, reach for the cup until shame turns to violence.

chapters.title: The bride seized
chapters.text: Eurytion tried to carry off the bride. Pausanias saw the scene on Athens' pediment: Peirithous in the centre, Eurytion seizing the wife of Peirithous, Caeneus bringing help, and on the other side Theseus defending himself against the centaurs with an axe — one centaur clutching a maid, another a youth in his prime. The Athenian hero was among the mightiest Nestor ever named beside Peirithous, Dryas, Caeneus, Exadius, and Polyphemus.

chapters.title: Caeneus and the pines
chapters.text: Apollodorus tells how Caeneus, once a woman granted invulnerability by Poseidon, killed many centaurs in the fight and scorned their wounds — until the survivors rallied with fir trees and buried him in the earth. Ovid names five centaurs he slew — Styphelus, Bromus, Antimachus, Elymus, and Pyracmos — before Latreus mocked the Lapith and the whole brood drove their living pillar down under the weight of pine.

chapters.title: Driven from Pelium
chapters.text: The Lapiths won the day. Homer remembers the aftermath in the Catalogue: on the day Peirithous got vengeance on the shaggy centaurs and thrust them from Pelium, glorious Hippodameia conceived Polypoetes to him — son whom Zeus begat, staunch in fight when Troy was besieged. The mountain that had housed Chiron and the wild brood would never again be wholly theirs; the centaur war entered art, epic, and the genealogies of Thessaly.
